title: Nested weighted integers
label: idb
statement: You are given a nested list: each element is an integer or a list whose elements may themselves be integers or lists. The **weight** of an integer is `maxDepth − depth + 1`, where depth counts from 1 at the top level and maxDepth is the deepest integer's depth. Return the sum of every integer multiplied by its weight.

stages.title: Inverse depth weighting
stages.say: You have a nested list of integers. An integer's weight is maxDepth minus its depth plus one — deeper means lighter. Return the weighted sum.
testNames: a deeper empty list does not change maxDepth: [1,[[]]] = 1

stages.title: Forward weighting
stages.say: Now the product team wants the opposite: weight equals depth, so deeper integers count more. Change as little as you can.
stages.require: Add `NestedWeights.DepthSum(nestedList)` where weight = depth (top level is 1).

flaw.ctx: You asked for the inverse-depth weighted sum in one pass.
flaw.answer: `levelSum` is reset every level, so each integer is added exactly **once** — this is the plain sum with weight 1, not inverse weighting. The running sum must carry across levels so shallow integers are re-added once per deeper level.
flaw.fix: Declare `levelSum` outside the loop (and handle levels holding only empty lists).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: You are given a nested list: each element is an integer or a list whose elements may themselves be integers or lists. The **weight** of an integer is `maxDepth − depth + 1`, where depth counts from 1 at the top level and maxDepth is the deepest integer's depth. Return the sum of every integer multiplied by its weight.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Does an empty list deeper than every integer count toward maxDepth? (No — only integers set the depth. The one-pass trick gets this wrong unless you handle it; the tests check `[1,[[]]]`.)
- Negative integers allowed? (Yes.)
- Can you do it in one pass without first finding maxDepth?

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Leaves deeper in the structure get less weight, so you don't know any weight until you have seen everything. Instead of two passes, keep a running sum of every integer seen so far and add it to the total once per level: an integer on level d is added (levels − d + 1) times, which is exactly its weight.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "O."ne BFS pass that adds the running sum of every level seen so far, once per level, weights each integer by its height from the bottom without computing the maximum depth first."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Two passes presented as one.
- Counting a level of only empty lists toward maxDepth — the one-pass running-sum trick does this by default ([1,[[]]] returns 3, not 1). The solution in this workspace's coding page had exactly this bug.
- Recursion on a very deep nesting.
- Resetting the level sum each level — that computes the forward weighting instead.

**Verification exercise:** Incorrect algorithm — `levelSum` is reset every level, so each integer is added exactly **once** — this is the plain sum with weight 1, not inverse weighting. The running sum must carry across levels so shallow integers are re-added once per deeper level.
